newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil stocks soaring, but for how long?.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil stocks soaring, but for how long?.

text.p: Brazilian shares have surged for several weeks in heavy trade, but equity analysts are beginning to question how long the market's bull run will last.
Bewildered at how fast and far the Sao Paulo bourse has risen this year, analysts were stunned Wednesday by a further 3.7 percent hike in South America's largest bolsa.
In just six months, the Sao Paulo bolsa's Bovespa index .BVSP has soared over 80 percent, more than double the rise most banks and consulting firms last January had projected for the entire year.

"The general climate remains optimistic...but the market has begun to question, with greater intensity, the higher risks of the large accumulated rise" in the bolsa, Lloyds Bank in Brazil said in a report.
"Even though the long-term outlook remains favorable, the risk that the market will gain higher volatility in the near future appears likely," it added.
While uneasy about the bolsa's surge, analysts see no sign the market will take a break from its rally as fresh money, particularly from domestic funds, continues to pour in.

"The year's rise so far is exaggerated, but it is hard to believe that the market will enter a profit-taking cycle soon," said a senior analyst at a U.S.-Brazilian asset management firm who asked not to be named.
Local investors, seeking higher returns, are moving to equity funds as fixed-income yields have dropped sharply due to the government's interest rate-cutting efforts.
Domestic equity fund assets have swollen to 17.2 billion reais from 6.7 billion reais in January, according to figures supplied by investment banks.
In May alone, local stock funds saw a net inflow of 3.19 billion reais. So far in June, net inflows have totalled 1.7 billion reais.
One result of the increased local buying has been ballooning trading volumes on local bourses.
Since May, daily bolsa trade has averaged between 800 million reais and more than a billion reais, way above the market daily average of just over 400 million reais in 1996.
"It is clearly a change in trading patterns and basically because of local players," said Manoel Maceira, asset manager at Banco Tendencia.

Recent news reports about the spectacular rise has helped boost stock prices, drawing in small local investors anxious to share in the profits of Brazil's bull market. Last week, the surge in the Sao Paulo bourse was the cover story of leading Veja weekly magazine.
"When the bolsa is on the front page of a magazine that sells more than one million copies, many small and medium-sized investors are tempted to join the game," a trader said.

Telecoms and power stocks have led the bolsa's rise due to the bright privatization prospects facing the sectors but demand from domestic equity funds has been the driving force behind the rises in second-tier issues.

"The rally began with blue-chips, particularly state companies up for privatization, but now funds are seeking to diversify by looking into other stocks and sectors," including food, banking, fertilizer producers and construction, he said.
A generally positive macroeconomic climate has also contributed to rising share prices. "There is no longer really bad (economic) news in Brazil," said an analyst.

Even concerns over Brazil's burgeoning current account deficit have been minimized. Analysts argue the current account gap, which this year is expected to reach $35 billion, can be managed as long as foreign direct investment keeps pouring in.
((--Sao Paulo newsroom 5511 2485412))
